name: Profit and Loss — Buying, Selling and the Percent That Matters
whatIsIt: Profit and Loss compares what something cost you (Cost Price, CP) to what you sold it for (Selling Price, SP). If SP is more than CP you made a profit; if SP is less than CP you made a loss. The exam trick is that profit% and loss% are ALWAYS calculated on the Cost Price, never on the selling price.
whyNeeded: Every shop, every trade, every 'we bought it cheap and sold it dear' story runs on this one idea. Competitive exams love it because a tiny wording change — 'profit on CP' vs a false-weight trick — flips the whole answer, so speed alone isn't enough; you need the right formula on autopilot.
realLifeUses: A shopkeeper pricing goods to make a target profit
Reasoning sections of SSC, banking and railway exams
Understanding markup vs margin in a family business
Working out real returns after buying and reselling anything — a phone, a cycle, shares

vocabulary.meaning: What the seller paid to get the item.
What the item was actually sold for.
SP − CP, when SP is bigger.
CP − SP, when CP is bigger.
The profit or loss written as a percentage of the Cost Price — always CP, never SP.

story.title: Ramu's Mango Cart
story.text: Ramu buys a crate of mangoes for ₹800 and sells the whole crate for ₹1000. 'I made ₹200,' he tells Divya proudly. She asks, 'Yes, but what's your profit PERCENT?' Ramu pauses — is it 200 out of 1000, or 200 out of 800? Divya explains: percent is always out of what you SPENT, the ₹800. So profit% = 200/800 × 100 = 25%. 'If you'd said 20% using the ₹1000, you'd have undersold your own hard work,' she laughs.
story.extractedProblem: CP = ₹800, SP = ₹1000. Find the profit percent.
story.answerInStory: 25% — profit ₹200 is calculated on the ₹800 cost price, not the ₹1000 selling price.

visual.caption: SP is the CP bar plus a profit slice on top — the slice, out of the CP bar, is the profit percent.

teachingGallery.title: Profit % is always on CP
teachingGallery.note: Draw the CP bar first, then show SP as CP plus (or minus) the profit (or loss) slice.

standardMethod.summary: Find CP and SP first. Profit or Loss = SP − CP (sign tells you which). Then Profit%/Loss% = (Profit or Loss ÷ CP) × 100. To go the other way — from a percent to SP — use SP = CP × (100 ± %) / 100.
steps: Identify CP and SP from the question.
Subtract: SP − CP. Positive means profit, negative means loss.
Divide the profit/loss by CP (never SP), then × 100 for the percent.
If asked for SP or CP given a percent, rearrange: SP = CP(100+P)/100 for profit, SP = CP(100−L)/100 for loss.

alternateMethods.name: 100-base shortcut
alternateMethods.whenToUse: When you're given a profit/loss percent and CP, and need SP fast.
steps: Profit p% means SP is (100+p) parts; loss l% means SP is (100−l) parts.

alternateMethods.name: False-weight trick
alternateMethods.whenToUse: A dishonest seller uses a lighter weight but charges for the full weight, at cost price.
steps: Profit% = (True weight − False weight) / False weight × 100.
This works because 'selling at cost price with less weight' is mathematically identical to profiting on the missing weight.
alternateMethods.example: Claims to sell 1000 g for the price of 1000 g, but the weight used is only 800 g → profit% = (1000−800)/800 × 100 = 25%.

workedExamples.problem: A book costs a shop ₹250 and is sold for ₹300. Find the profit percent.
A cycle bought for ₹4000 is sold at a loss of 12%. Find the selling price.
A trader sells goods at 15% profit for ₹4600. Find the cost price.

trickPractice.intro: Every profit% or loss% question is (difference ÷ CP) × 100 — CP is the base, always.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calculating profit% or loss% using the Selling Price as the base instead of the Cost Price.
commonMistakes.fix: Percent is ALWAYS out of the Cost Price — that's the money that was actually risked. 'Profit on SP' is a different (and much rarer) question type.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mixing up which of CP/SP is bigger, so profit gets called loss or vice-versa.
commonMistakes.fix: SP > CP is profit; SP < CP is loss. Write SP − CP first — the sign tells you instantly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using SP = CP × (100+p)/100 when going backward from SP to CP, forgetting to flip the fraction.
commonMistakes.fix: Forward (CP known): SP = CP × (100±p)/100. Backward (SP known): CP = SP × 100/(100±p) — the 100 always sits with whichever price you DON'T know.

medium.q: SP ₹460 at a loss of 8%. Find CP.
A pen bought at ₹40 is sold at ₹34. Find loss%.

challenge.q: A shopkeeper claims to sell at cost price but uses a weight of 900 g for every 1000 g billed. Find his profit%.
An item is sold at 20% profit; had it been sold for ₹40 more, the profit would have been 30%. Find the CP.
Goods sold at 10% loss instead of 10% profit fetch ₹40 less. Find CP.

questions.q: SP is less than CP — this is called a…
A radio bought for ₹1200 is sold for ₹1500. Profit%?

teachBackPrompt: Teach a friend why profit% is always calculated on the Cost Price and never the Selling Price, using the ₹800-mango-crate story where profit is ₹200 but the percent is 25%, not 20%.

revisionCard.summary: Profit/Loss = SP − CP (positive = profit, negative = loss). Percent is ALWAYS (Profit or Loss ÷ CP) × 100 — CP is the base. Forward: SP = CP(100±%)/100. Backward: CP = SP × 100/(100±%). False-weight trick: profit% = (true weight − false weight)/false weight × 100.

gameMission.title: The Fair-Price Market
gameMission.brief: Help traders in the jungle market price their goods correctly — always measure profit against what they spent, not what they earned!

realLifeProject: Pick 3 items around your home and imagine reselling them. Decide a fair selling price for a 15% profit on what they'd have cost new, and show your CP/SP/profit% working.

meta.curriculum: Competitive reasoning (Quantitative Aptitude) — Profit and Loss

rememberIt.unpack: Profit or Loss ÷ CP × 100 — never divide by SP.

studentQuestions.q: Why isn't the percent calculated on the Selling Price?
studentQuestions.a: Because CP is what was actually invested — the percent measures the RETURN on that investment. Using SP would understate every profit and overstate every loss.

studentQuestions.q: What's the fastest way to find SP from CP and a profit percent?
studentQuestions.a: SP = CP × (100 + profit%)/100. Treat CP as 100 parts and scale up (or down for a loss) in one multiplication.
